name: Oxendolone

card.summary: A steroidal antiandrogen injected in Japan for enlarged prostate, discussed in appearance circles as an androgen-receptor blocker relevant to androgen-driven hair thinning.
card.note: Marketed only in Japan, by injection; not a hair-loss product.

quick.overview:
Oxendolone is a synthetic steroid that blocks the androgen receptor and also acts on the progesterone receptor. It was introduced in Japan in 1981 for benign prostatic hyperplasia and is given by intramuscular injection [1].

Its link to appearance is by mechanism: androgen-receptor blockers are the drug class that people looking at androgen-driven traits such as hair thinning study. No trial of oxendolone for hair or skin was located; published human studies concern the prostate.
quick.how: It is a prescription drug used in Japan under brand names such as Prostetin, given by intramuscular injection under medical supervision. It is not effective by mouth because oral bioavailability is very low [1].
quick.risks: Reported effects follow from antiandrogen and progestin action, and one Japanese study of antiandrogens for prostate enlargement examined effects on blood lipids [7]. It is marketed only in Japan.

lead: Oxendolone is a steroidal antiandrogen and progestogen, also known by the code TSAA-291, introduced for medical use in Japan in 1981 as a treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia [1]. It is given by intramuscular injection, and a human metabolism study found slow excretion with a plasma half-life of about 5 to 6.6 days after injection [6].

In looks-related discussion, it sits in the hair category as an androgen-receptor blocker, a class that works against the hormonal drivers of male-pattern hair loss and acne. Published human research on oxendolone itself concerns the prostate, not hair or skin.

chain: Reduces androgen signalling in target tissues
Class relevant to androgen-driven hair thinning
angle.text: Interest in oxendolone comes from its mechanism as an androgen-receptor antagonist. No hair-loss trial of the drug has been published.

paras: Its approved use is benign prostatic hyperplasia. A randomized comparison in Japan tested oxendolone, an alpha-blocker (bunazosin) and both together, with the combination showing the highest improvement rate at twelve weeks [2]. A 1984 case series reported subjective improvement in 83% of 43 patients on weekly injections [8].

Laboratory work found oxendolone binds the androgen receptor and inhibits testosterone 5-alpha-reductase in tumour tissue [4]. In rats, it suppressed exercise-induced muscle hypertrophy, which the authors took as a sign that androgen signalling contributes to training adaptation [5].

A study of men on antiandrogens for prostate enlargement, including oxendolone, followed lipid changes over twelve months [7]. Another report on oxendolone noted a significant fall in VLDL with little change in other lipids [8].

No studies of oxendolone for hair loss or skin were found. In prostate research, a randomized triple-blind trial of 60 men found weekly injections raised urinary flow but not significantly more than placebo [3].

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use in Japan [1].
